title: Calling in sick (Krankmeldung)
summary: Tell your boss or your teacher that you're ill, by email or by phone, in the right form.
goals: Write a short email: greeting, reason, what happens next, closing
Choose Liebe/Lieber or Sehr geehrte/Sehr geehrter
Know the basic rules for being ill at work in Germany

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 17: Health (Gute Besserung!)

points: Five conjunctions sit at 'position 0': [[und]], [[aber]], [[oder]], [[denn]], [[sondern]]. They join two main clauses without counting as a position, so the verb stays second in both.

[[und]] (and) and [[oder]] (or): when the subject (and verb) are the same, drop them in the second part: [[Ich esse einen Hamburger und trinke einen Saft.]], [[Ich nehme eine Pizza oder ein Sandwich.]]
[[aber]] (but) always gets a comma before it: [[Ich möchte eine Smartwatch kaufen, aber sie ist so teuer.]]
[[sondern]] (but rather) comes after a negative with [[nicht]] or [[kein]], with a comma: [[Das ist kein Buch, sondern eine Schokolade.]], [[Sie kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.]]
[[denn]] (because) gives a reason, with a comma, and keeps its subject: [[Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ich will in Deutschland studieren.]]

points: Say them differently: [[den]] has a long e, [[denn]] a short e, [[dann]] an a.
[[den]] is an article: masculine accusative ([[Ich suche den Autoschlüssel.]]) and dative plural ([[in den neuen Büchern]]).
[[denn]] means because and joins two sentences: [[Ich esse eine Pizza, denn ich habe Hunger.]]
In questions, [[denn]] is a little word that adds interest or surprise and has no translation: [[Was machst du denn hier?]], [[Wann hast du denn Zeit?]]
[[dann]] means then: one thing after another ([[Zuerst spielen wir, dann schlafen wir.]]), later on, or 'in that case'.

sections.title: A short email in four parts
sections.text:
1. **Greeting.** People you know: [[Liebe Frau Weber,]] (a woman), [[Lieber Herr Müller,]] (a man), or [[Hallo Eva,]] for friends. Formal: [[Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,]] / [[Sehr geehrter Herr Müller,]], and [[Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,]] when you don't know the name.
2. **After the comma**, the next line starts with a small letter: [[leider bin ich heute krank.]]
3. **The reason and what happens next:** [[Ich habe Fieber und kann heute nicht kommen. Ich gehe heute zum Arzt.]]
4. **Closing:** [[Viele Grüße]] (friendly) or [[Mit freundlichen Grüßen]] (formal), with no comma after it (unlike English), and your name on the next line.

[[Liebe]] / [[Lieber]] and [[geehrte]] / [[geehrter]] change with the person's gender. Learn them as fixed openings; adjective endings come at A2.

items.en: I have a temperature and a headache.

sections.title: The rules in Germany
sections.text: Tell your employer **on the first day**, before work starts. If you're ill for more than three days, you usually need a doctor's note ([[die Krankschreibung]]); some employers want it from the first day. With public health insurance, the doctor sends it electronically to your insurance, and your employer gets it from there.

Russian Уважаемая ... and Armenian Հարգելի ... are like [[Sehr geehrte ...]]: formal. Russian Дорогая ... is like [[Liebe ...]], but German uses [[Liebe]] much more widely, also for a boss or a teacher you know.

items.question: You're writing to your boss, Ms Weber, whom you know well. How do you start?
items.explanation: Liebe for a woman you know; Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren only when you don't know the name.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: Unfortunately I'm ill today.
items.explanation: leider takes position 1, so the verb comes next: Leider bin ich ...

items.question: Which closing is formal?
items.explanation: Mit freundlichen Grüßen is formal; Viele Grüße is friendly.

items.prompt: I can't come to work today.
answers: Ich kann heute nicht zur Arbeit kommen
Heute kann ich nicht zur Arbeit kommen
Zur Arbeit kann ich heute nicht kommen
items.explanation: kann in second place, kommen at the end; zur Arbeit = zu der Arbeit.
